title: HL extension: the role of culture
summary: How culture shapes cognition, the self, mental health, development and relationships, and how to study culture without bias.

keyterms.definition: Seeing the self as separate and defined by personal traits; more common in individualist cultures.
Seeing the self as defined by relationships and roles; more common in collectivist cultures.
Attending to context and relationships between objects; associated with East Asian cultures in Nisbett's research.
Focusing on objects and their attributes separate from context; associated with Western cultures.
Judging behaviour by the standards of its own culture rather than another.
Judging other cultures by the norms of one's own.
Using concepts or tools developed in one culture as if they were universal.
Passing cultural knowledge and norms from one generation to the next.

questions.prompt: Masuda and Nisbett (2001) showed underwater scenes to Japanese and American participants. Japanese participants:
options: Mentioned the background and context more
questions.explanation: This supports cultural differences in holistic versus analytic attention.

questions.prompt: Markus and Kitayama (1991) proposed that in many collectivist cultures the self is:
questions.explanation: Interdependent self-construal defines the self through relationships.

questions.statement: Levine et al. (1995) found people in more individualist countries were more likely to say love was essential for marriage.
questions.explanation: Participants in collectivist countries such as India and Pakistan were more willing to marry without love.

questions.statement: Using a Western depression questionnaire everywhere without testing whether it fits local meanings is an imposed etic.
questions.explanation: This risks missing culturally specific expressions of distress.

questions.text: Judging another culture by the standards of your own is ___.
questions.explanation: Ethnocentrism is a source of cultural bias in research.

questions.text: Focusing on objects separate from their context is ___ thinking.
questions.explanation: Nisbett linked analytic thinking to Western cultures.

questions.prompt: Match each finding to the context it informs.

pairs.left: Levine et al. (1995): love and marriage

questions.explanation: The culture extension runs across all four contexts.

questions.prompt: Why should cultural differences in studies like Masuda and Nisbett (2001) be interpreted carefully?
options: They describe group tendencies, with large individual variation within cultures
They apply to every person in a culture
questions.explanation: Overgeneralizing group findings to individuals leads to stereotyping.

questions.prompt: Which approach best avoids cultural bias when studying mental health in a new community?
options: Use a translated Western questionnaire only
Begin with emic interviews to understand local concepts, then design measures
questions.explanation: Combining emic and etic approaches reduces imposed etic bias.

questions.prompt: Order a culturally sensitive research process.
items: Consult local researchers and community members
Use emic methods to explore local concepts
questions.explanation: Comparison is only fair once measures mean the same thing in each culture.

questions.prompt: Van IJzendoorn and Kroonenberg (1988) found relatively more insecure-resistant infants in:
questions.explanation: Childrearing practices, such as little separation from mothers in Japan, may explain this.

questions.prompt: Bond and Smith (1996) found conformity was higher in collectivist cultures. A cultural explanation is that:
options: Agreeing with the group may be seen as tactful and valued
questions.explanation: Behaviour that looks like "conformity" may reflect cultural values.

questions.statement: Cultural relativism means behaviour should be judged using the norms of the culture where it occurs.
questions.explanation: This reduces ethnocentric bias in interpreting behaviour.

questions.statement: Culture only affects social behaviour, not perception or memory.
questions.explanation: Research such as Masuda and Nisbett (2001) and Cole and Scribner (1974) shows culture affects cognition.

questions.text: Passing cultural norms from one generation to the next is called cultural ___.
questions.explanation: Transmission happens through enculturation and social learning.

questions.text: Seeing yourself mainly through relationships and roles is an ___ self-construal.
questions.explanation: Markus and Kitayama (1991) introduced this distinction.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its meaning.

pairs.right: Judging others by your own culture
Judging by the culture's own norms
Treating one culture's tools as universal

questions.explanation: These ideas are central to the concept of bias in cross-cultural research.

questions.prompt: An HL synthesis question asks about culture and treatment of depression. Which point shows the strongest understanding?
options: Treatments may need adapting to local beliefs about the causes of distress, and stigma affects help-seeking
Only drugs work in collectivist cultures
questions.explanation: Culturally adapted interventions consider beliefs, language and stigma.

questions.prompt: Which is a limitation of using nations as "cultures"?
options: Nations contain many subcultures, so averages hide variation
questions.explanation: Within-country variation can be as large as between-country variation.

questions.prompt: Order how culture might influence attachment, according to cross-cultural research.
items: Childrearing practices (e.g. how often infants are separated)
questions.explanation: Differences in classification may reflect practices rather than poorer bonds.
